skill.name: Hyperbole
skill.why: Writers stretch the truth on purpose to make a feeling big, or funny.
skill.how: Find the part that can't be true. Ask what it really means, and why.

steps.say: I packed my own school bag today. Here's my moan.
steps.ask: Could a school bag really weigh that much?

check.nudge: A thousand kilos is heavier than a car. Could you carry a car to school?

steps.win: No way! I made it bigger. That's stretching the truth.

steps.say: Shrink it back to normal size.

options.text: My bag is really heavy.

options.reason: Then why would I moan? I'm saying the opposite of empty.

steps.win: Yes! A huge stretch on purpose is called hyperbole.

steps.say: Hyperbole isn't a lie. We both know I'm stretching.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote a letter to the island ranger. A Whopskip is peeking over her shoulder.
encounters.text:
Dear Ranger Tan,

This morning I found a pelican tangled in fishing line near the boardwalk. Its wing was caught, and it couldn't fly. I phoned your office at eight o'clock. Then I waited forever for you to come. I sat on the boardwalk, talking quietly to the pelican so it would stay calm. The mosquitoes ate me alive. When you arrived just before ten, you cut the line in about two seconds. The pelican flapped once, looked at us, and flew off. Thank you for coming in the end, even if my legs are now one big itchy bump.

Wren

options.reason: The ranger did come, just before ten, and cut the line.

encounters.frame: Gus has left his lab diary open on the galley table. The Whopskip is holding its nose.
encounters.text: Lab diary, Day 34. The Stink Sock is ready. I have worn this sock for five weeks without washing it, including three footy games and one very sweaty bushwalk. Today I opened the jar for the first time. The smell could melt the paint off a battleship. Mo, who was standing two metres away, sat down on the deck without a word. A seagull flying overhead turned around and went back the way it came. Zed said his eyebrows were trying to leave his face. I have put the lid back on and wrapped the jar in three plastic bags. I wrote down every reaction in my notebook, with times. At 9:02, Mo sat down. At 9:03, the seagull left. At 9:05, Wren opened every porthole on the boat and asked me, very politely, never to do that again. Next step: test it on Maxx's guards. That's not gross. That's science.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote a match report on the Reef Rays for the island newsletter.
encounters.text: REEF RAYS SNEAK HOME. What a game! The Reef Rays played the Mudflat Magpies on Saturday in front of a big crowd. Each quarter went for twenty minutes, plus a bit of time on. After three quarters, the Rays were behind by two points. Then came the last quarter, which lasted about three weeks. The Magpies kicked a goal. The Rays kicked one back. Nobody could breathe. With one minute left, our full-back made a smother so brave that the crowd gasped, and our rover snapped the winning goal from a tight angle. The siren went, and the Rays had won by four points. I chewed my scarf so hard during that quarter that it now has holes in it. The coach said afterwards that it was the bravest team effort she had seen all season. Next week the Rays play the Pelican Point Pirates, who are top of the ladder.

encounters.frame: Gus told the crew about his night walk. Wren was there too. The Whopskip is hiding under the table.
encounters.text:
Last night Gus walked the boardwalk after dark, and Wren went with him. This morning he told the crew all about it at breakfast. Wren wrote down what really happened.

GUS: I walked the whole boardwalk alone. My torch went out halfway along. I was so scared that my hair turned white and fell out. My heart was thumping so hard they could hear it in the city. Then something jumped out at me, and I chased it right off the boardwalk!

WREN'S NOTES: I held Gus's hand the whole way, because he asked me to. His torch did go out, so we used mine. Near the end, a mudskipper flopped onto the boards in front of us. Gus screamed and ran all the way back to the boat. This morning his hair is still brown and still on his head. It just needs a wash.

encounters.success: Hyperbole wants you to spot it. A fib, like walking alone, wants you to believe it. Wren's notes catch fibs.

encounters.text:
INTRODUCING MAXXPODS GOLD: THE ONLY HEADPHONES THAT MATTER.

parts: LIFE IN THE MUD. Most visitors hurry along the Mirage Mangroves boardwalk, swatting insects and holding their noses. If you slow down, though, the mud is full of surprises. At low tide, look closely at the edge of the water and you will see mudskippers.

parts.tap: These small fish can breathe air and stay out of the water for hours, as long as their skin stays damp.
parts.reason: It sounds amazing, but Wren gives the condition: damp skin. That's a careful fact, not a stretch.

parts.tap: I watched one climb a mangrove root and sit there like a lookout.
parts.reason: That's a simile, not a stretch. A mudskipper really can sit on a root and watch.

parts: Next to them, hundreds of fiddler crabs wave their claws.

parts.tap: The ranger measured one male whose big claw was almost as long as the rest of his body.
parts.reason: The ranger measured it. A surprising fact can still be true.

parts: The males wave them to show off. The trees are just as clever. Their roots poke up out of the mud, so the tree can breathe when the tide is high. One tree can drop hundreds of seedlings, which float away on the tide to start new forests. I wanted a photo of a mudskipper jumping, so I crouched beside a burrow with my camera ready.

parts.tap: I waited about a hundred years before one finally popped out.

parts: It skipped right over my shoe.

parts: Most of them never notice the mudskippers at all. Bring insect spray, wear long sleeves and walk slowly. The mud is worth a closer look.

encounters.frame: Mo wrote Gus an apology letter. Tully wrote what each hyperbole does, but got one part wrong.
encounters.text:
Dear Gus,

I am writing to say sorry about your slime experiment. I know you have been working on it since roughly the beginning of time, and I know it was meant to win the Island Science Fair. When I saw the bucket of green goo in the galley, I honestly thought it was lime jelly. I was so hungry that I could have eaten the entire boat, including the anchor, so I grabbed a spoon.

I only had one mouthful. It tasted like a swimming pool full of old socks. I have brushed my teeth four hundred times since then, and my tongue is still green. I am so sorry that I will probably never sleep again.

To make it up to you, I have bought you a new bucket and three bottles of glue, and I will clean the galley every night for a week. I have also written a sign for the bucket that says NOT JELLY in capital letters. Please forgive me. You are my best mate in the whole history of the universe.

Mo

encounters.frame: Zed posted about Swamp Dash Level 50 on the crew chat. The Whopskip helped, by sitting on the controller.
encounters.text: Crew, I have finally beaten Level 50 of Swamp Dash, and I need to tell you about it. First of all, the final boss, a giant robot crocodile, could take a hit from a volcano and keep smiling, and every jump needed perfect timing, down to a millionth of a second. I'm fairly sure I started this level when dinosaurs were still around. While I was waiting for the last checkpoint to load, my apple went mouldy and then turned into soil. Gus brought me a sandwich when I started, and by the time I finished, he had grown a long grey beard. When I finally landed the last hit, I cheered, and people in New Zealand covered their ears. The controller buzzed, and every sleeping baby in Victoria woke up. For the record, the level has twelve checkpoints, three hidden keys and a lava bridge that collapses if you stand still. I found two keys on my own and the third with a guide. Tully says I owe her a new pair of earmuffs. Now I'm going to lie down for about a decade.

encounters.frame: The Mirage Mangroves surf club pinned up this report. The Whopskip can't swim in surf, so it's just reading.
encounters.text:
SURF REPORT: OUTER BAR, SATURDAY. A strong southerly swell arrived overnight, and by seven o'clock the waves on the outer bar had reached about three metres, measured from the club tower. Sets were rolling in every eleven seconds, with a nasty rip running out beside the rocks at the northern end. The water temperature had dropped to sixteen degrees, so most surfers wore full wetsuits and booties.

Only the most experienced club members paddled out, and not a single surfer caught a wave before nine, because the sets were breaking so fast and so close together. At around ten, club veteran Bev Nguyen caught the wave of the morning. From the top of it, she could have waved to the passengers on passing planes, and she rode it all the way to the sand without falling off once. The crowd on the beach cheered and blew their whistles.

By lunchtime, the wind had swung round to the north-east and the swell was easing. The red and yellow flags are back up, and the club barbecue starts at two.

encounters.success: Waving to planes is a stretch. Surfers deciding whether to paddle out need the real height, not a joke.

options.reason: Waves vary, so 'about' is honest. It was measured from the club tower, a real reading.

'Not a single surfer caught a wave before nine': it might scare surfers.
options.reason: It's true, and the report explains why. Honest facts about danger help surfers stay safe.

options.text: 'A nasty rip running out beside the rocks': the word 'nasty' is too emotional.
options.reason: The rip really is dangerous. A strong word warns surfers, and it's true, not a stretch.

encounters.frame: A page from a young astronaut's training diary has washed up in the mangroves.
encounters.text:
Training diary, Week 12. Today was the day I'd been dreading since I first signed up: the spinning chair. It's a seat on the end of a long metal arm that whirls you round and round to test how much your body can take before you black out or throw up. The instructor strapped me in and gave me a paper bag, which did not make me feel any better.

The moment the arm started to turn, my stomach dropped about forty floors. After one minute, my cheeks were pulled back so far that I could see my own ears. After two minutes, I'm fairly sure my brain had swapped places with my lunch. The instructor's voice came through the headset, calm and slow, telling me to breathe, but I couldn't remember how breathing worked. Six minutes felt like six hundred years.

When the arm finally stopped, I sat there with my eyes shut while the room kept spinning without me. I didn't need the paper bag, which my instructor said makes me one of only three trainees this year. Tomorrow I have to do it again. I am going to eat a very small breakfast.

options.text: It lets the reader feel how awful the spinning was.
It tells the reader exactly how fast the chair spun.

options.text: It shows the reader the writer was badly hurt.
options.reason: The writer sits with closed eyes, then plans to go again tomorrow. Nobody was hurt.

options.text: It makes the reader want a go on the chair.
options.reason: The writer was dreading it and plans a tiny breakfast. That doesn't sell the ride.
